\title{Does Per-Token Routing Help Tiny Hybrid Language Models?\\
A Budget-Matched Two-Corpus Study and a Normalization Audit}

\author{Anonymous submission}

\begin{document}
\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
Hybrid language models that blend neural networks with $n$-gram statistics
conventionally use a few fixed, corpus-level weights
\cite{mikolov2011,sundermeyer2012}. We test whether replacing every fixed
weight with a \emph{learned per-token router} helps in the small-footprint
regime that on-device applications occupy, routing among six frozen experts (a
Kneser-Ney trigram, two recency bigrams, a 512-token cache, a continuation
unigram, and a 3.3--8.2M-parameter GRU) on WikiText-2 and the Penn Treebank
under one aligned-scoring protocol. We report two results. First, a
methodological one that applies to any gated mixture: our initial version of
this study found a 27--33\% perplexity win for the router, and the win was an
artifact of the evaluation, not of the model. The router's
``vote'' features were the experts' probabilities \emph{of the word being
scored}, so its weights depended on the candidate; the resulting mixture summed
to 2.66 (WikiText-2) and 2.56 (PTB) over the vocabulary instead of 1, and every
router perplexity was deflated by that factor. A one-line vocabulary-mass audit exposes
this, and we release it as a guard. Second, the corrected result: with strictly causal
features and a \emph{budget-matched} protocol (router, static mixture and
interpolation weight all tuned on validation only), a 15.5\,KB router buys
13.2\% (WikiText-2) and 5.3\% (PTB) perplexity over tuned two-expert
interpolation, but only 1.1\% and 2.2\% over a tuned static mixture of the
same six experts --- and the same router trained on the training stream is
\emph{far worse} than both (250.8 and 138.2), because expert reliability is
not stationary between the stream the experts were built on and held-out text.
The tuned static hybrid itself is the real win at this footprint: 119.1 and
89.7 at 68.7 and 28.7\,MB, better than the GRU alone (146.9/103.0) and than a
KenLM 5-gram (250.9/138.4). All code, logs, and the invalidated artifacts are
released.
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}

Mixture architectures with learned routing are among the oldest ideas in neural
computation \cite{jacobs1991,jordan1994} and now scale to frontier models
\cite{shazeer2017}. We claim no architectural novelty. We ask a question the
literature has not answered at the \emph{bottom} of the footprint range: when
every expert is a frozen classical statistic plus one small recurrent network,
does learned per-token routing beat the tuned fixed interpolation that
practitioners actually deploy?

The fixed-weight answer is settled at larger scales: interpolating a neural LM
with Kneser-Ney smoothing using one or a few heldout-tuned weights has been
standard practice for over a decade
\cite{mikolov2011,sundermeyer2012,chang2015}. At those scales the neural
component dominates, so the blending scheme is a detail. In the
small-footprint regime---on-device, offline, CPU-only personalization
\cite{mathur2023}---the blending scheme is one of the few levers left, and
nobody has checked whether per-token routing changes the conclusion there.

We ran that experiment twice. The first run said yes, emphatically: a 13.5\,KB
router appeared to cut perplexity by 33\% (WikiText-2) and 27\% (PTB) relative
to tuned fixed interpolation, at every seed, on two corpora. The result was
wrong, and the way it was wrong is the first contribution of this paper
(\S\ref{sec:audit}). The router's input included, for each expert, the
probability that expert assigned to the \emph{gold} next word. Those features
were literally the labels: \texttt{X[:, :5]} was bit-identical to
\texttt{L[:, :5]} in the collected dataset. Because the weights therefore
depended on the word being scored, the ``mixture'' was not a probability
distribution --- summing it over the vocabulary gave 2.66 (WikiText-2) and
2.56 (PTB) instead of 1.000, while every baseline row summed to 1.000. Router
perplexities were deflated by exactly that factor; normalized, the same trained
router scores $\approx$240 and $\approx$174, i.e.\ \emph{worse} than the tuned
interpolation it appeared to beat by a third, and worse than the GRU alone.

\S\ref{sec:audit} turns that failure into a cheap, reusable audit. The rest of
the paper reports the corrected experiment, in which the router sees only
causal, candidate-independent evidence: each expert's confidence in its own
favourite word, whether the five favourites agree, and 14 context statistics.

\paragraph{Findings.} On two corpora under one aligned protocol, with every
tuned component given the same budget (validation data only):
\begin{itemize}\itemsep0pt
\item \textbf{Candidate-conditioned gating is not a language model.} Its
  vocabulary mass is $>$1, its perplexity is deflated by that mass, and the
  ``hindsight oracle'' it is usually compared to is deflated too. A sum-to-one
  check (\S\ref{sec:audit}) catches the whole class of bug in one line.
\item \textbf{Per-token routing helps a little, not a lot.} A valid-tuned
  15.5\,KB router reaches 117.9 (WT-2) and 87.8 (PTB), versus 135.8/92.7 for
  tuned two-expert interpolation ($-13.2\%$/$-5.3\%$) and 119.1/89.7 for a
  tuned static mixture of the same six experts ($-1.1\%$/$-2.2\%$; three
  seeds, sd 0.06 on PTB).
\item \textbf{Training the router on train is a trap.} The same architecture
  trained on the 10--13$\times$ larger training stream scores 250.8 (WT-2) and
  138.2 (PTB) --- worse than uniform mixing (182.6/138.4) and worse than every
  tuned static baseline. Expert reliability shifts sharply between the stream the
  statistical experts were built on and held-out text (KN3: 34.7 $\rightarrow$
  165.1 PP from PTB train to test), and a train-fit router memorizes that
  shift (\S\ref{sec:why}).
\item \textbf{The hybrid, not the routing, is the win.} A tuned static mixture
  of five cheap experts and a small GRU reaches 119.1 (WT-2) / 89.7 (PTB) at
  68.7/28.7\,MB --- better than the GRU alone (146.9/103.0), than tuned
  two-expert interpolation (135.8/92.7 is close on PTB) and than a toolkit
  KenLM 5-gram (250.9/138.4).
\end{itemize}

We release the full stack---every expert, the router, the aligned protocol, the
audit scripts, the seed audits, and the \emph{invalidated} v1 artifacts with
the code that produced them---so that both the result and the mistake are
checkable.\footnote{Code, logs, and the full reproduction pipeline are anonymized for review and will be released upon acceptance.} The system is
named \textsc{Hedge} in the repository after the prediction-with-expert-advice
lineage \cite{freund1997}; the router itself is a supervised MLP, not
multiplicative weights.

\section{Related Work}

\paragraph{Interpolated language models.} Linear interpolation of probability
estimates originates with \citet{jelinek1980} and was systematized by Kneser-Ney
smoothing \cite{kneser1995} and its empirical study \cite{chen1999}. Our
trigram expert follows this line; our interpolation \emph{weights} are the
object of study.

\paragraph{Fixed-weight neural/$n$-gram hybrids.} Neural probabilistic LMs
\cite{bengio2003}, and RNN and LSTM LMs in particular, have long been
interpolated with Kneser-Ney models using heldout-tuned fixed weights
\cite{mikolov2010,mikolov2011,sundermeyer2012}; \citet{chang2015} discriminatively train a
handful of context-dependent scaling factors---the closest classical relative
of our router, at ASR scale and with features that do not include the scored
word's own probabilities. Our baselines are exactly this family.

\paragraph{Mixture of experts.} Gating networks date to \citet{jacobs1991} and
\citet{jordan1994}; sparse routing at scale to \citet{shazeer2017}. That
lineage learns routers for \emph{trainable} experts at footprints orders of
magnitude above ours. A gate that reads the candidate's own expert scores is
unobjectionable in discriminative reranking of an $n$-best list, where the score
is never required to be a normalized distribution; the failure mode we document
is carrying that construction into perplexity.

\paragraph{Prediction with expert advice.} Online bounds against the best
expert in hindsight \cite{freund1997,cesabianchi2006} motivate the
per-position-best-expert diagnostic. We stress that this diagnostic is
\emph{not} a realizable bound for a mixture LM (\S\ref{sec:audit}).

\section{System and Protocol}
\label{sec:system}

\paragraph{Experts.} Six experts, all frozen after fitting: (1) a modified
Kneser-Ney trigram (discount scale 1.15, shared across corpora); (2--3) lag-2
and lag-3 recency bigrams; (4) a 512-token adaptive cache; (5) a continuation
unigram; (6) a word-level GRU (vocabulary $+$1; 3.3M parameters on PTB, 8.2M
on WT-2; Adam, cosine schedule, best-by-validation checkpoint; batchified
perplexity 86.3 on PTB, 119.2 on WT-2).

\paragraph{Router.} A one-hidden-layer MLP with a softmax over the six
experts. Its 24 input features are a function of the \emph{context only}: five
expert confidences $\log p_i(\hat w_i(\mathrm{ctx}))$ where $\hat w_i$ is
expert $i$'s own favourite word, five agreement flags (does expert $i$'s
favourite equal the plurality favourite), and 14 context statistics (Kneser-Ney
backoff mass and continuation counts, recency-bigram totals and hit flags, two
age-invariant cache densities, a 4-way backoff-bucket one-hot, position in
sentence, sentence-start flag). Hidden size $h \in \{24,64,128,256\}$ gives a
2.9--31.0\,KB router. Training minimizes the mixture's negative log-likelihood
by Adam over collected aligned features.

\paragraph{The invariant.} Because the weights $\alpha(\mathrm{ctx})$ do not
depend on the scored word, $P(w\mid\mathrm{ctx}) = \sum_i \alpha_i
p_i(w\mid\mathrm{ctx})$ sums to 1 over the vocabulary whenever each expert does
(unit-tested). Every perplexity we report is a perplexity.

\paragraph{Aligned scoring.} All systems score \emph{one shared gold token
stream} per corpus at exactly the positions the router sees
($\sum_s \mathrm{len}(s)-1$ per split), so every row of every table is
comparable by construction. Sentence-initial targets and \texttt{eos} are
excluded; this makes our numbers systematically \emph{higher} than batchified
literature numbers for the same model, and we therefore never compare against
published perplexities directly.

\paragraph{Budget-matched tuning.} Every tuned component gets validation data
and nothing else: the interpolation weight $\lambda^{*}$ of the classical
two-expert hybrid ($p = \lambda p_{\mathrm{KN3}} + (1-\lambda)
p_{\mathrm{GRU}}$; $\lambda$ is therefore the \emph{trigram} weight) from a
201-point grid on validation ($\lambda^{*}=0.21$ on WT-2, $0.28$ on PTB ---
the trigram earns a larger share on the smaller corpus); the static mixture $\alpha$ by EM/gradient on validation; the
router's hidden size by 2-fold cross-validation \emph{inside} validation and
its weights by fitting validation. Fitting on the training stream is reported
separately as a negative control, because the training stream is the corpus the
statistical experts were built from.

\section{The Audit: Candidate-Conditioned Gating Is Not an LM}
\label{sec:audit}

A gated mixture is a distribution only if its weights are a function of the
context. If the gate reads anything about the word $w$ being scored, then
\begin{equation}
Z(\mathrm{ctx}) \;=\; \sum_{w \in V} \sum_i \alpha_i(x_{\mathrm{ctx},w})\,
p_i(w\mid\mathrm{ctx}) \;\neq\; 1,
\end{equation}
and $\exp\bigl(-\tfrac1N\sum \log P(w_t)\bigr)$ is not a perplexity: it is
deflated by roughly $\exp(\overline{\log Z})$. Nothing in the training loop
signals this --- the objective decreases, the validation curve looks healthy,
and the model can even ``beat'' a hindsight oracle, because the oracle
$\max_i p_i(w_t)$ has the same defect.

\paragraph{Measurement.} We enumerate $Z$ over the full vocabulary at randomly
sampled aligned test positions, with the cache streamed causally so its state
matches evaluation (\path{benchmarks/normalization_audit.py}). On the v1
leaky router: $Z = 2.66$ (WT-2) and $2.56$ (PTB); the per-position
best-expert ``oracle'' reaches $Z \approx 3.1$. On KN3, the GRU and the
fixed-interpolation baseline: $Z = 1.000$. On the corrected causal router:
$Z = 1.000$ by construction and by measurement.

\paragraph{Consequence.} Table~\ref{tab:audit} restates the v1 headline. The
deflation factor is almost exactly the size of the claimed win, which is why
the artifact survived three seeds, two corpora, an ensemble and a size sweep:
all of them inherited the same features.

\centering\small
\setlength{\tabcolsep}{4pt}
\begin{tabular}{lrrr}
\toprule
router & reported & mass $Z$ & $\times Z$ \\
\midrule
WT-2, v1 (leaky) & 90.3 & 2.66 & $\approx$240 \\
PTB, v1 (leaky) & 68.0 & 2.56 & $\approx$174 \\
WT-2, corrected & 117.9 & 1.000 & 117.9 \\
PTB, corrected & 87.8 & 1.000 & 87.8 \\
all baselines & --- & 1.000 & --- \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{The v1 artifact. ``Reported'' is the full-test perplexity the
protocol printed; $Z$ is the mean vocabulary mass measured at 100--150 sampled

reported number becomes once each position is normalized by its own $Z$. On the
same samples the audit prints the pair directly (WT-2 v1: 120.2 $\rightarrow$

each other and not to the router. ``All baselines'' = KN3, the GRU,
fixed-$\lambda$ and static-$\alpha$.}
\label{tab:audit}
\end{table}

\paragraph{The guard.} Two checks now run in the test suite and in the
regeneration pipeline:
(i) \texttt{gate\_hybrid.load\_split} refuses to start if any feature column of
the collected dataset is bit-identical to any label column;
(ii) \texttt{tests/test\_gate.py} asserts that two streams sharing a context
but differing afterwards produce \emph{identical} feature rows, that each
expert sums to 1 over the vocabulary, and hence that any context-only mixture
does too. This is the same discipline that caught an earlier Witten-Bell
baseline whose distribution summed to $>$1 and whose perplexity was deflated by
it; sum-to-one is not a nicety, it is the precondition for comparing rows.

\paragraph{The router wins, barely (Table~\ref{tab:money}).} Against the
classical two-expert baseline and with an identical tuning budget, per-token
routing over all six experts cuts perplexity by
13.2\% (WT-2, 117.9 vs.\ 135.8) and 5.3\% (PTB, 87.8 vs.\ 92.7) relative to
tuned two-expert interpolation --- but by only 1.1\% (117.9 vs.\ 119.1) and
2.2\% (87.8 vs.\ 89.7) relative to a tuned static mixture of the same six
experts. On PTB the gap to static mixing is 1.94 PP against a router seed sd of
0.06, so it is real but small; on WT-2 it is 1.28 PP against a seed sd of 0.29. The honest reading is that most of the gain over
classical interpolation comes from \emph{having six experts and tuning their
global weights on held-out data}, not from reweighting them per token: the
static mixture alone recovers 171.0 $\rightarrow$ 119.1 on WT-2 and 101.7
$\rightarrow$ 89.7 on PTB, and the router adds 1--2\% on top.

\paragraph{Without the GRU, routing does help --- over uniform.} Restricting
the router to the five statistical experts (valid-tuned) gives 194.5 (WT-2) and
132.8 (PTB), against 263.9 and 196.2 for uniform mixing of the same five. So
the router learns something real about when to trust a trigram over a cache or a
recency bigram; it is just that a tuned global mixture already captures most of
the available gain once a strong neural expert is in the pool.

\paragraph{Router size does not matter.} Sweeping $h \in \{24,64,128,256\}$
for the train-trained router (WT-2 test 263.6/254.2/263.7/250.8; PTB
141.2/138.2/138.3/144.8) gives a flat, noisy curve whose 13\,PP spread on WT-2
exceeds every effect we claim. For the valid-tuned router, 2-fold CV on
validation is flat too (WT-2 CV valid 122.42/122.37/\textbf{122.08}/122.16;
PTB 92.71/92.52/\textbf{92.18}/98.27) and picks $h=128$ (15.5\,KB) on both
corpora. An earlier version of this work reported corpus-dependent optima
(13.5\,KB on WT-2, 2.6\,KB on PTB); that curve was a property of the leaky
features, not of the corpora.

\paragraph{Seeds.} The valid-tuned router is stable: WT-2 $118.06\pm0.29$
(ensemble 117.60) and PTB $87.84\pm0.06$ (ensemble 87.74) over three seeds,
against static baselines that are deterministic to two decimals ($119.14\pm
0.01$, $89.71\pm0.00$). The router's margin over static mixing, seed-mean to seed-mean, is 1.08 PP
($\approx$3.7 router-sd) on WT-2 and 1.87 PP ($\approx$31 sd) on PTB. The train-trained negative
control is reported at a single seed; its instability is the point, and the
four-size sweep is its spread.

\paragraph{Selective expert activation does not survive the correction.} The
router's GRU weight is computed from context alone, so thresholding it is a
free, causal skip rule, and under the v1 protocol it appeared to run the GRU on
47--55\% of tokens for $\le$0.5 PP. With the corrected router the GRU carries
most of the weight nearly everywhere: even at $\tau=0.5$ it is still consulted
on 99.0\% (WT-2) and 89.7\% (PTB) of tokens, at 118.1 and 89.9 PP. The cost
lever was an artifact of the same leak.

\section{Why Routing Does Not Transfer}
\label{sec:why}

\begin{table}[t]
\centering\footnotesize
\setlength{\tabcolsep}{4pt}
\begin{tabular}{lrrr}
\toprule
 & train & valid & test \\
\midrule
\multicolumn{4}{l}{\emph{PTB: each expert's own perplexity}} \\
KN3 trigram & 34.7 & 178.1 & 165.1 \\
lag-2 bigram & 135.8 & 1{,}335.0 & 1{,}220.3 \\
cache (512 tokens) & 1{,}739.4 & 1{,}780.2 & 1{,}615.7 \\
lag-3 bigram & 177.5 & 2{,}035.6 & 1{,}879.1 \\
cont.\ unigram & 1{,}048.6 & 1{,}048.7 & 992.0 \\
GRU & 46.6 & 111.8 & 103.0 \\
\midrule
\multicolumn{4}{l}{\emph{PTB: mixtures}} \\
router (train-trained) & 20.6 & 146.8 & 138.2 \\
\quad its mean weights, static & 29.8 & 112.3 & 105.4 \\
uniform weights & 46.4 & 144.5 & 138.5 \\
static (valid-fit) & 32.7 & 94.0 & 89.7 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{The mechanism (\texttt{router\_diagnostic.py}). Expert
reliability is not stationary: every statistical expert is far stronger on the
stream it was built from (KN3 34.7 $\rightarrow$ 165.1), while the GRU shifts
much less (46.6 $\rightarrow$ 103.0). A train-fit router learns per-context
trust in experts that stop being reliable; using its \emph{own average} weights
statically already recovers most of the damage (138.2 $\rightarrow$ 105.4), so
the per-context modulation is what mis-transfers.}
\label{tab:shift}
\end{table}

Table~\ref{tab:shift} isolates the failure. Two facts matter. First, the
statistical experts are not merely weaker on held-out text, they are
\emph{differently} weak: the trigram degrades $4.8\times$ from its own training
stream while the GRU degrades $2.2\times$, so the trust allocation that is
optimal on train is wrong on test. Second, the train-trained router's
\emph{mean} weights, frozen and applied statically, score 105.4 on PTB test
versus the router's own 138.2 per-context decision: the average is fine, the
modulation is not. Validation tuning sidesteps the whole problem, which is why
the budget-matched protocol is not a formality here --- it is the difference
between a router that helps (87.8) and one that costs 57\% more perplexity
than it should on PTB (138.2) --- and 113\% more on WT-2 (250.8 vs.\ 117.9).

\paragraph{Cost.} One torch thread, 200 test sentences, 7 interleaved rounds,
median quoted; the harness now asserts that no system measures faster than a
component it contains --- the check the v1 cost table failed, having timed the
GRU alone at 5.09\,ms/token and the hybrid containing it at 3.60. WT-2, in
ms/token: GRU alone 4.21, two-expert interpolation 4.26, the same six experts
mixed statically 4.32, routed hybrid 4.89. Routing therefore costs $+0.57$
ms/token in situ ($+13.2\%$), and 0.44 ms/token measured in isolation
(features $+$ MLP, no GRU) $=9.0\%$ of the hybrid. On PTB, where the GRU is
$5\times$ cheaper, the same rows are 0.78 / 0.85 / 0.88 / 1.46: routing costs
$+0.58$ ms/token ($+66\%$) and 0.31 ms/token in isolation ($21\%$ of the
hybrid). Evaluating the four extra experts is nearly free ($+0.04$ to $+0.06$
ms/token); the router is not. The KN3 top-1 memo is cleared every round, so
these rows are worst-case for routing. Energy is a wall-time $\times$ 15\,W TDP
proxy, not measured power. Read with the quality rows: routing costs 13--66\%
more per token than statically mixing the same experts, for 1--2\% perplexity.

\section{Limitations}

(1) \emph{Scale}: WT-2 and PTB are small corpora and our absolute numbers are
not comparable to published ones (our protocol excludes sentence-initial
targets and \texttt{eos}; batchified evaluation of the same GRU gives 119.2 /
86.3). We claim only the controlled comparison. (2) \emph{Feature set}: our
causal features are confidences, agreement flags and count statistics. A router
given richer causal evidence --- expert top-$k$ identities as embeddings,
per-expert entropies --- might extract more; we did not test that, and at this
footprint the flat size sweep suggests features, not capacity, are the
binding constraint. (3) \emph{Experts}: all six are frozen; joint training
changes the reliability-shift story of \S\ref{sec:why} and is the obvious next
step. (4) \emph{Baselines}: no transformer expert, one tokenizer, two English
corpora, CPU timing on one machine. (5) \emph{Effect size}: the router's
advantage over a tuned static mixture (2.2\% on PTB, 1.1\% on WT-2) is small
enough that seed variance matters: three seeds give $118.1\pm0.3$ (WT-2) and
$87.84\pm0.06$ (PTB) for the router against $119.14\pm0.01$ and
$89.71\pm0.00$ for static mixing, so the effect is a few standard deviations,
not orders of magnitude.

\section{What This Says About Routing at Scale}
\label{sec:scale}

The reason to care about routing at this footprint is the same reason to care
about it at any footprint: spend the expensive component only where it pays.
Three preconditions had to be met here before that question could even be asked,
and all three are cheap to check at any scale.
\begin{itemize}\itemsep0pt
\item \emph{Normalization.} A router that sees the candidate's own scores
  produces a score, not a distribution (\S\ref{sec:audit}). One line settles
  it: $\sum_w P(w\mid\mathrm{ctx})$.
\item \emph{Budget-matched baselines.} A tuned static mixture of the same
  experts is a far stronger opponent than a single tuned $\lambda$ (119.1 vs.\
  135.8 on WT-2, 89.7 vs.\ 92.7 on PTB). Most of what looks like ``routing
  wins'' is ``six experts beat two''.
\item \emph{Stationarity.} The router must be tuned on a stream whose
  expert-reliability profile matches deployment, or its per-context trust
  mis-transfers (\S\ref{sec:why}). This is the one that costs 57--113\%
  perplexity when ignored.
\end{itemize}
The cost side does not vanish at scale either: routing is 9--21\% of per-token
latency here for 1--2\% perplexity, and a skip rule built on the router's own
weight for the expensive expert found almost nothing to skip (99.0\%/89.7\%
usage at $\tau=0.5$), because an honestly tuned router wants the strong expert
nearly everywhere. Whether that changes when the expensive expert is a
transformer layer --- where the cost asymmetry is orders of magnitude larger and
the cheap experts are relatively much weaker --- is the question this study is
meant to inform. We deliberately do not extrapolate to it.

\section{Conclusion}

At the bottom of the footprint range, learned per-token routing over frozen
classical experts plus one small GRU buys a few percent over a tuned static
mixture of the same experts, and a double-digit percent over classical
two-expert interpolation --- provided the router is tuned on held-out data, and
provided its features are causal. Trained on the training stream it is worse
than uniform mixing. The larger lesson is methodological: a gate that reads the
scored word's own probabilities produces an unnormalized ``language model''
whose perplexity is deflated by the vocabulary mass, and that mass was 2.56--2.66
in our own first run --- enough to manufacture a 27--33\% win out of nothing,
complete with three seeds, two corpora, an ensemble and a size sweep that all
agreed. Sum-to-one is a one-line check. Run it.

The cost side is equally unflattering: routing adds 0.57--0.58\,ms/token in
situ over statically mixing the same six experts (+13\% on WT-2, +66\% on PTB,
where the GRU is cheap), for a 1--2\% perplexity gain. At this footprint the
deployed answer is the tuned static hybrid; the router is a research result
about where per-token decisions do and do not pay.

\section{Reproduction}

\texttt{bash scripts/run\_paper\_pipeline.sh \{wt2|ptb\}} regenerates every
router-dependent number for one corpus: causal feature collection, the leak
guard's unit tests, the main results table with the size sweep, the seed audit,
selective activation, the reliability diagnostic, the cost harness, both
normalization audits (current and v1), and the footprint metadata. The GRU
expert and its aligned scores are inputs
(\path{nn_expert.py --score-only}); the KenLM and 5-gram baselines
are router-independent (\path{benchmarks/kenlm_baseline.py},
\path{benchmarks/fix_5gram.py}). \texttt{HEDGE\_RESULTS} switches every
artifact path between corpora.

\section{The Invalidated v1 Numbers}

For the record, the v1 protocol (router features \texttt{[0:5]} = the scored
word's expert log-probabilities, \texttt{[12]} = its cache count; static
mixture fit on train; ``oracle'' = per-position best expert) produced, on
217{,}004 / 75{,}623 aligned positions: 5-expert router 99.7 / 72.7; 6-expert
router 90.3 / 68.0 ($h=128$ / $h=24$, three-seed mean $101.1\pm21.2$ /
$74.6\pm10.1$, ensembles 90.2 / 69.9); valid-trained router $81.5\pm4.1$ /
$70.7\pm12.1$; static mixture 171.0 / 101.7; tuned interpolation 135.8 / 92.7;
per-position best expert 57.4 / 44.4. Every router row is invalid
(unnormalized, $Z\approx2.6$); the per-position-best row is unnormalized and
was never a bound; the static row was fit on train while its competitors were
tuned on validation (valid-fit: 119.1 / 89.7). Only the tuned-interpolation row
survives unchanged, which is precisely why it looked like a baseline being
beaten by a third. The artifacts, the
logs, and the code that produced them (commit \texttt{9d2eac4}) are kept under
\path{benchmarks/results/*/legacy_leaky_v1/} with a README stating exactly
this, and \path{benchmarks/normalization_audit.py --legacy} re-measures the
deflation from them.
